newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Leftist rebels shut down key Colombian pipeline.
newsitem.headline: Leftist rebels shut down key Colombian pipeline.

text.p: Leftist rebels attacked a key oil pipeline in northeast Colombia, shutting it down for the second time in less than a week in a crippling blow to the country's oil infrastructure, authorities said on Wednesday.

A spokesman for the state oil company, Ecopetrol, said the latest attack on the Cano Limon-Covenas pipeline occurred on Tuesday afternoon in northeastern Arauca province, near Colombia's border with Venezuela.

He said it was not immediately clear how much oil had been spilled in the blast, but all pumping operations had been suspended along the 220,000-barrel per day pipeline since about 2 p.m. local time (1900 GMT) Tuesday.

The structure carries oil from the Cano Limon field operated by Occidental Petroleum Corp Plc to the Caribbean port of Covenas. It was attacked 46 times by suspected National Liberation Army (ELN) guerrillas in 1995 and has been dynamited 37 times so far this year.
Tuesday's attack occurred shortly after repairs had allowed for the reopening of the pipeline following a weekend attack by ELN saboteurs in Norte de Santander province.
The ELN, Colombia's second largest guerrilla group, was founded by radical Roman Catholic priests in 1966 and specializes in kidnappings and economic sabotage.
It has managed to bring transportation across much of Colombia to a standstill since last Friday when it announced a nationwide offensive against the government of President Ernesto Samper.

Army commander Gen. Harold Bedoya has complained that about half of his 120,000 troops work full-time guarding oil and coal facilities and that he lacks the manpower to wage an effective counterinsurgency campaign.

Government officials said earlier this week that they planned to call up members of the 120,000-strong military reserves to help counter the growing rebel threat. But Juan Carlos Ramirez, head of the National Planning Department, told reporters Tuesday that the cash-strapped government had no funds to pay for the additional troops.
